doc.title: Bob Cranshaw interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

chapter: Church, energy and the state of jazz
title: Young musicians, managers and the lost culture of standards
summary: Record companies and managers steer young stars away from older players and standards, and his generation scattered into leaders instead of playing together.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: guys coming out of the schools and so forth but I think that management and the music business has taken another look at it and said — hmmm, people are starting to like jazz. All those commercials I hear, everything is jazz now you know. And it’s a money making situation and most of the kids have no idea, they’re not in touch with the culture. With Josh Redman and so forth, Josh never has the time to spend with some older players or to see the older players, because they’re already moved aside, because of money or because of management. If you call and you want to get a younger player on a record date, you’ve got to go through the manager to get him, which is okay because music is music business. I mean I also talk to kids, it is music is music business regardless to whether you’re involved in classical playing or whatever, it is still a business. But we just looked at it as music. I mean we hoped that we were able to make money to feed our families from what we were doing, but it was fun. It was more fun at that time I think. And it’s hard for me, my son is a bass player and it’s hard for me to relate. I tell him stories but those stories don’t hold true to the younger guys now, that the guys when I was working with Joe Williams and we were around the Basie band. The experiences and stories that these guys were living and talking about, I couldn’t wait to experience the same things. You know, when is it my turn? You know, right now, the younger guys don’t have the time, don’t have the chance to get into any of that. If they seem to be a little above the norm, they’re taken and put to the side, and then they start their careers. Somebody else tells you this is where your career is going. This is what you do, this is what you should do. So we don’t have a hands-on and they don’t have a chance to play with enough people or to work, enough experiences. They come out and they’re stars. The younger guys know very little tunes. They know the tunes that they write. But as far as knowing music, they don’t know you know, we came up through an era where people wrote originals, but we had so many lovely standards. I mean so many great tunes out there, you know I wish I were a writer but I’m still trying to get to those great things that have already been written. You know the Broadway show tunes and all of these things. The kids don’t have any idea. They don’t know. And when they find them or they hear them, they’re busy trying to be an individual to the tune until it takes it somewhere else. So they never get the essence of what that tune is about. They just kind of hear it and then they’re gone. Because they’re driven to have to come up with something. Don’t do what he did. Don’t be like him. Don’t do, you know, it’s this kind of thing. So they never connect in that way, which may be the fault of my era of guys, ‘cause we kind of split up. The older guys, the Milt Hintons and people stuck together. We kind of started to get a little notoriety and then we scattered like somebody threw a bomb in and we all moved. We don’t play together enough you know. This guy forms this group and you never hear Sonny Rollins, Max Roach or those group of guys really playing together any more. They all became leaders.
